commonErrors.example: A learner writes on the worksheet that a velocity-time graph running flat at 12 m/s means the object has stopped, picking the statement that a flat line always means zero velocity.

fixIt.corrected: Corrected working: the height of the line is the velocity, so flat at 12 m/s means the velocity never changes - the object keeps moving at the same speed.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: say what the height of a flat velocity-time line tells you and what the object at 12 m/s is doing.

commonErrors.misconception: A flat line on a velocity-time graph means the object has stopped.

commonErrors.example: On the exit ticket, a learner answers that an object whose velocity-time graph runs flat at 8 m/s has stopped.

fixIt.corrected: Corrected check: a flat v-t line means constant velocity: the object keeps moving at the same speed - flat at 8 m/s, it covers 8 metres every second.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: give the one-sentence correction for the claim that a flat line on a velocity-time graph means the object has stopped.

commonErrors.misconception: A flat line on a velocity-time graph means the object has stopped.

modelAnswers.question: A distance-time graph climbs 120 metres in 60 seconds in a straight line. What is the speed, and how does the graph show it?
A distance-time graph climbs 90 metres in 30 seconds in a straight line. What is the speed?

nextSteps: Reteach the trap with the flat line held at a steady height, landing that the height of the line is the velocity and a flat line means it never changes.
Practise the check from the worked example - trace the graph step by step: gradient of the distance-time graph first, then slope and area on the velocity-time graph.
strengths: Most of the class can calculate speed from distance and time, such as reading the athlete's 100 metres in 20 seconds as a speed of 5 metres per second.
The class can read a distance-time gradient as speed and the area under a velocity-time graph as the distance travelled.
